subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A term newborn is noted to be cyanotic at birth with a single loud S2. Echocardiography shows a single large arterial trunk arising from the base of the heart that gives rise to the coronary arteries, the pulmonary arteries, and the systemic circulation, with a large ventricular septal defect.
question: Failure of development of which of the following structures is the most likely cause of this infant's condition?

options.text: Spiral partitioning of the truncus by the conotruncal (spiral) septum
Formation of the aorticopulmonary septum
Fusion of the endocardial cushions
Closure of the ductus arteriosus after birth
Fusion of the septum primum with the septum secundum

explanation_correct: This infant has persistent truncus arteriosus, a right-to-left shunt in which the truncus arteriosus fails to divide into the pulmonary trunk and aorta because the aorticopulmonary septum fails to form. A single vessel then receives blood from both ventricles, and most patients have an accompanying ventricular septal defect. It is one of the 5 T's of early-cyanosis ('blue baby') congenital heart disease, which are often diagnosed prenatally or immediately after birth and usually require urgent surgery and/or prostaglandin therapy to maintain ductal patency.

explanation_incorrect.A: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral produces D-transposition of the great arteries, in which there are two switched vessels (aorta from the right ventricle, pulmonary trunk from the left ventricle), not a single common trunk.
explanation_incorrect.C: Failure of endocardial cushion fusion causes septal and atrioventricular canal defects (ostium primum ASD, VSD, AVSD), classically associated with Down syndrome, not a single arterial trunk.
explanation_incorrect.D: Failure of ductal closure produces a patent ductus arteriosus, which is acyanotic at presentation with a continuous machine-like murmur, not a single great vessel with early cyanosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Failed fusion of the septum primum and septum secundum produces a patent foramen ovale, which is distinct from a true septal defect and is usually asymptomatic.

educationalObjective: Persistent truncus arteriosus results from failure of aorticopulmonary septum formation and is usually accompanied by a VSD, presenting as early cyanosis in a newborn.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 2-day-old term boy has profound cyanosis and tachypnea. There is a single loud S2 and no significant murmur. Chest x-ray shows a narrow superior mediastinum with an 'egg on a string' appearance. Echocardiography shows the aorta arising anteriorly from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk arising posteriorly from the left ventricle.
question: Which of the following best explains the embryologic basis of this infant's findings?

options.text: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
Complete failure of aorticopulmonary septum formation
Failed fusion of the septum primum with the septum secundum
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
Downward displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets into the right ventricle

explanation_correct: This infant has D-transposition of the great arteries, caused by failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral. The aorta leaves the right ventricle (anteriorly) and the pulmonary trunk leaves the left ventricle (posteriorly), creating parallel systemic and pulmonary circulations. The condition is not compatible with life unless a shunt (VSD, PDA, or patent foramen ovale) allows mixing of blood, and the failed spiral produces the narrow superior mediastinum ('egg on a string') on chest x-ray. Without surgical intervention, most infants die within the first few months of life.

explanation_incorrect.A: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum is the mechanism of tetralogy of Fallot, which produces pulmonary infundibular stenosis, RVH, an overriding aorta, and a VSD rather than transposed great arteries.
explanation_incorrect.B: Complete failure of aorticopulmonary septum formation causes persistent truncus arteriosus, a single vessel, whereas this patient has two vessels that arise from the wrong ventricles.
explanation_incorrect.C: Failed fusion of the septum primum and secundum causes a patent foramen ovale, which in this patient could serve as a mixing shunt but is not the primary defect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Downward displacement of tricuspid valve leaflets 'atrializing' the right ventricle is Ebstein anomaly, associated with lithium exposure in utero, not transposition of the great arteries.

educationalObjective: D-transposition of the great arteries results from failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral, causing aorta-RV and pulmonary trunk-LV connections that require a mixing shunt for survival.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A newborn girl is cyanotic from the first hours of life. Echocardiography shows absence of the tricuspid valve and a hypoplastic right ventricle. ECG shows tall P waves in lead II indicating right atrial hypertrophy and left axis deviation consistent with left ventricular hypertrophy.
question: Which of the following anatomic findings is most likely required for this patient's survival?

options.text: Coexisting ASD plus VSD or PDA to allow shunting and maintain cardiac output
A large isolated PDA as the only route of systemic blood flow
Ductal patency maintained solely by prostaglandin E synthesis and low O2 tension
An overriding aorta straddling a ventricular septal defect
A left-to-right shunt through the VSD that increases pulmonary blood flow

explanation_correct: Tricuspid atresia is the absence of the tricuspid valve with a hypoplastic right ventricle; because no blood can pass from right atrium to right ventricle, viability requires both an ASD (to shun systemic venous return leftward) and a VSD or PDA (to deliver blood to the lungs). The ECG characteristically shows right atrial hypertrophy (tall P waves) and left ventricular hypertrophy with left axis deviation, as seen here.

explanation_incorrect.B: A PDA alone does not provide an intra-cardiac route for right atrial blood to reach the left side of the heart; an ASD is also required for systemic venous return to bypass the absent tricuspid valve.
explanation_incorrect.C: Prostaglandin E and low O2 tension maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus, but ductal patency alone cannot sustain circulation in tricuspid atresia, which requires an ASD as well.
explanation_incorrect.D: An overriding aorta straddling a VSD is a feature of tetralogy of Fallot, not of tricuspid atresia.
explanation_incorrect.E: In tricuspid atresia the necessary shunts function right-to-left to maintain cardiac output; a left-to-right shunt increasing pulmonary flow is the physiology of uncorrected L-to-R defects, which here would not bypass the absent tricuspid valve.

educationalObjective: Tricuspid atresia (absent tricuspid valve, hypoplastic RV, tall P waves and left axis deviation on ECG) requires both an ASD and a VSD/PDA for viability.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 3-year-old boy with known tetralogy of Fallot becomes intensely cyanotic and dyspneic while crying during a vaccination. A caretaker picks him up and he instinctively assumes a squatting position, after which his cyanosis gradually improves.
question: Which of the following best explains why squatting improves this patient's cyanosis?

options.text: It decreases pulmonary vascular resistance, increasing antegrade flow through the stenotic pulmonary outflow tract
It increases venous return to the right atrium, which enlarges the right-to-left shunt across the VSD
It increases systemic vascular resistance, which decreases the right-to-left shunt across the VSD
It decreases systemic vascular resistance, which reduces right ventricular afterload
It compresses the overriding aorta, directing more blood into the pulmonary circulation

explanation_correct: In tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary stenosis forces right-to-left flow across the VSD, and 'tet spells' are precipitated by crying, fever, and exercise, which exacerbate RV outflow obstruction. Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance, which decreases the right-to-left shunt and thereby improves cyanosis. The tetrad (PROVe) comprises Pulmonary infundibular stenosis, RVH (boot-shaped heart), Overriding aorta, and VSD.

explanation_incorrect.A: Squatting does not lower pulmonary vascular resistance; the improvement comes from raising systemic resistance, which reduces the right-to-left shunt rather than increasing antegrade pulmonary flow.
explanation_incorrect.B: Increasing the right-to-left shunt would deliver more desaturated blood to the systemic circulation and worsen cyanosis, the opposite of what squatting achieves.
explanation_incorrect.D: Decreasing systemic vascular resistance would favor right-to-left shunting across the VSD and worsen the tet spell.
explanation_incorrect.E: Squatting does not compress or reorient the overriding aorta; the hemodynamic benefit is mediated by increased systemic vascular resistance.

educationalObjective: Tet spells in tetralogy of Fallot are triggered by crying, fever, and exercise, and squatting improves cyanosis by increasing SVR and decreasing the right-to-left shunt.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 6-month-old boy has a history of cyanotic episodes with crying. Examination shows a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border and a single loud S2. Chest x-ray shows a boot-shaped heart. Echocardiography confirms right ventricular hypertrophy, a large VSD, an overriding aorta, and marked narrowing of the right ventricular outflow tract.
question: Which of the following features of this patient's defect is the most important determinant of his prognosis?

options.text: Degree to which the aorta overrides the ventricular septal defect
Size of the ventricular septal defect
Degree of right ventricular hypertrophy
Boot-shaped appearance of the heart on chest x-ray
Severity of the pulmonary infundibular stenosis

explanation_correct: This child has tetralogy of Fallot, caused by anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum and the most common cause of early childhood cyanosis. Within the PROVe tetrad, pulmonary infundibular stenosis is explicitly the most important determinant of prognosis, because it governs the degree of right-to-left shunting across the VSD and hence the severity of cyanosis and tet spells.

explanation_incorrect.A: The overriding aorta straddles the VSD and receives blood from both ventricles, but it is not the primary determinant of prognosis in tetralogy of Fallot.
explanation_incorrect.B: A VSD is one of the four components of the tetrad, but its size is not the most important prognostic factor; the outflow tract stenosis is.
explanation_incorrect.C: Right ventricular hypertrophy is a consequence of pulmonary stenosis forcing right-to-left flow, a secondary finding rather than the prognostic driver.
explanation_incorrect.D: The boot-shaped heart on chest x-ray reflects right ventricular hypertrophy and is a descriptive imaging sign, not a prognostic determinant.

educationalObjective: In tetralogy of Fallot (PROVe), the degree of pulmonary infundibular stenosis is the most important determinant of prognosis.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 1-day-old term girl is cyanotic and tachypneic. Echocardiography shows that all pulmonary veins drain into the right heart circulation (into the SVC and coronary sinus) rather than the left atrium, along with an atrial septal defect. She is started on prostaglandin infusion while surgical repair is arranged.
question: Which of the following best explains how this infant is able to maintain systemic cardiac output?

options.text: The pulmonary veins deliver oxygenated blood directly into the left ventricle through the coronary sinus
Right-to-left shunting through the ASD (and sometimes a PDA) allows mixed blood to reach the systemic circulation
A left-to-right shunt across the ASD increases pulmonary blood flow and raises systemic arterial saturation
The ductus arteriosus shunts aortic blood into the pulmonary trunk, which reoxygenates it before it enters the descending aorta
An overriding aorta receives blood from both ventricles, providing adequate oxygen delivery

explanation_correct: In total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR), the pulmonary veins drain into the right heart circulation (SVC, coronary sinus, etc.), so all systemic and pulmonary venous blood mixes in the right atrium. An associated ASD — and sometimes a PDA — allows right-to-left shunting to maintain cardiac output, which is why the ASD is essential for survival and why prostaglandins may be used to maintain ductal patency. TAPVR is one of the 5 T's of early-cyanosis congenital heart disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: In TAPVR the pulmonary veins do not reach the left atrium or left ventricle at all; drainage into the coronary sinus is precisely the anomaly, not a mechanism of oxygen delivery.
explanation_incorrect.C: A left-to-right shunt across an ASD is the physiology of an uncomplicated atrial septal defect; in TAPVR the required shunt is right-to-left to deliver any oxygenated blood systemically.
explanation_incorrect.D: Flow through a PDA in TAPVR permits right-to-left (aortic-to-pulmonary) mixing to support pulmonary flow, not reoxygenation of aortic blood before it reaches the descending aorta.
explanation_incorrect.E: An overriding aorta straddling a VSD is a component of tetralogy of Fallot, not of total anomalous pulmonary venous return.

educationalObjective: TAPVR requires an ASD (± PDA) so that mixed venous blood can shunt right-to-left and maintain cardiac output; it presents with early cyanosis.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 17-year-old boy presents with recurrent palpitations and a narrow-complex tachycardia with a short RP interval. His mother reports taking lithium for bipolar disorder throughout her pregnancy with him. Echocardiography shows apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets with 'atrialization' of the right ventricle and moderate tricuspid regurgitation.
question: Which of the following additional features is most likely associated with this patient's congenital anomaly?

options.text: Bicuspid aortic valve with progressive aortic root dilation
Supravalvular aortic stenosis with characteristic facial features
Juxtaductal narrowing of the aorta with upper-extremity hypertension
Accessory conduction pathways causing tachyarrhythmias and right-sided heart failure
Overriding aorta with right ventricular outflow obstruction and tet spells

explanation_correct: Ebstein anomaly is the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets into the right ventricle, artificially 'atrializing' the ventricle. It is associated with tricuspid regurgitation, accessory conduction pathways (which cause the recurrent supraventricular tachyarrhythmias seen here), and right-sided heart failure. It is rare and can be caused by lithium exposure in utero, as in this patient's history.

explanation_incorrect.A: A bicuspid aortic valve is associated with coarctation of the aorta and Turner syndrome, not with lithium exposure or tricuspid valve displacement.
explanation_incorrect.B: Supravalvular aortic stenosis is the cardiac defect of Williams syndrome and does not involve the tricuspid valve.
explanation_incorrect.C: Juxtaductal aortic coarctation causes upper-extremity hypertension with weak, delayed lower-extremity pulses and is associated with Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve.
explanation_incorrect.E: An overriding aorta with right ventricular outflow obstruction describes tetralogy of Fallot, a cyanotic defect of the infundibular septum rather than the tricuspid valve.

educationalObjective: Ebstein anomaly (downward-displaced tricuspid leaflets atrializing the RV) is associated with tricuspid regurgitation, accessory conduction pathways, right-sided HF, and prenatal lithium exposure.
